item.title: The Fold — 2026-11-14
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 14 November 2026: Overloaded air traffic routers trigger the longest US nationwide flight ground stop since 9/11 as Microsoft apologises for a global 365 outage, the White House announces a three-way nuclear summit between Trump, Putin and Xi in China, the Met Police open a criminal inquiry into David Walliams, and disclosures reveal Trump bought millions in Nvidia shares while loosening China export rules.
item.content:encoded:
Saturday 14 November 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Overloaded air traffic control routers force the longest US nationwide flight ground stop since 11 September 2001 as Microsoft apologises for a 24-hour global outage across Outlook and Teams.
  • Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping plan a three-way nuclear arms summit in Shenzhen next week while European leaders warn against Russian peace traps and Iran targets a US radar in Bahrain.
  • The Metropolitan Police launch a criminal investigation into David Walliams over alleged serious sexual offences as probation officers vote for industrial action and Downing Street weighs wider disability benefit reforms.
  • Brazil’s Senate approves a R$56bn fiscal adjustment package while a rejected Federal Police report links Supreme Court justices Alexandre de Moraes and Kassio Nunes Marques to Banco Master owner Daniel Vorcaro.
  • Financial disclosures reveal Donald Trump bought millions of dollars in Nvidia shares while loosening China export rules, as the International Energy Agency declares the start of the age of electricity at Cop31.
  • Artificial intelligence unlocks hundreds of proved theorems in Kurt Gödel’s shorthand notebooks and OpenAI launches a payment wallet for AI agents, while a tearful Mauricio Pochettino leaves the US national team for Manchester United.

News

Overloaded routers trigger longest US nationwide flight ground stop since 9/11 as Microsoft apologises for global 365 outage

The US Federal Aviation Administration lifted the longest nationwide ground stop in American aviation since 11 September 2001 on Friday evening after a telecommunications failure across all Air Route Traffic Control Centers halted takeoffs for over four hours. Ordered at 3.54pm Eastern Time and lifted at 8.15pm, the freeze delayed over 9,100 flights and cancelled nearly 8,000 while leaving 3,500 airborne aircraft to land or divert. At the FAA’s request, Eurocontrol suspended US-bound departures across its 42 member states—including the UK, EU, Ukraine, Turkey and Israel—while Sydney Airport grounded transpacific flights. (Guardian, BBC, The Verge)

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin ruled out a cyber-attack or any connection to the week’s Microsoft disruption, blaming ageing analogue switches and routers in Terminal Radar Approach Control facilities that overloaded with data and fed inconsistent radar and radio information to controllers. The failure began in Chicago before cascading to Boston, Washington, New York and Minneapolis after a reported update and reboot on contractor L3Harris’s private network. Air Space Intelligence denied any link to its new $875m cloud-based SMART system, while Duffy urged Congress to fund a full replacement of US air traffic infrastructure. (Guardian, The Verge)

The aviation halt capped a day of digital paralysis after Microsoft apologised for a nearly 24-hour global outage across Microsoft 365—hitting Outlook, Teams, Word, Excel, SharePoint, OneDrive and Copilot—that generated 130,000 incident reports across 74 countries. Serving 430 million users and over 90% of Fortune 500 firms, the platform suffered server configuration errors during a capacity upgrade that caused machines to fail automated health checks and knocked out connectors used by OpenAI and Anthropic. In the UK, NHS hospitals, GP surgeries and schools faced disruption, several police forces asked the public to report crimes by telephone, and National Rail warned that emailed tickets might be inaccessible. (Guardian, BBC, The Verge)

Worldwide, the Microsoft failure stalled legislative business in the US House of Representatives, disrupted rail alerts and hospital email in Canada, and hit government systems in Japan, Singapore, France, Australia and the Philippines. In Brazil, Supreme Federal Court President Edson Fachin, acting as head of the National Council of Justice, granted an emergency request from the Brazilian Bar Association to suspend procedural court deadlines until Monday 16 November after state courts in São Paulo and Santa Catarina reported widespread tool failures. (BBC, Folha)

Trump, Putin and Xi plan three-way nuclear talks in China as Europe warns of Russian peace traps and Iran targets US radar in Bahrain

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping plan to hold an unprecedented trilateral summit next week on the sidelines of the Apec gathering in Shenzhen to discuss nuclear arms reduction and Iran, White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales announced on Friday. Trump will attend Tuesday’s Asean summit in the Philippines before arriving in China on Wednesday for a fourth bilateral meeting with Xi on Thursday, followed by the three-way talks with Putin. Although US officials expect no formal agreement, the meeting comes nine months after the last US-Russia nuclear treaty expired in February, leaving the largest atomic arsenals without guardrails as Trump seeks a pact covering Beijing. (BBC)

Ukraine is not on the Shenzhen agenda, and at an EU summit in Dublin on Friday foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas warned Western capitals against Russian traps after Moscow used Abu Dhabi talks to revive its December 2021 demands to halt Nato enlargement and roll back forces in eastern Europe. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen rejected any overhaul of Europe’s security architecture, while European Council President António Costa announced a joint European negotiating team combining the EU with Britain, France, Germany, Italy and Poland. In Kyiv, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said speed curbs on SpaceX’s Starshield network persist along the entire front line, hampering Shahed drone interceptions as Russian strikes hit a Kyiv hospital and killed three people in Zaporizhzhia and Odesa, while car bombs in Moscow and St Petersburg killed a Russian colonel and injured former Ukrainian aide Sergei Zavorotniy. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian)

In the Gulf, Iran’s Revolutionary Guards claimed they destroyed a US early-warning radar in Bahrain in retaliation for a US strike on a tower in Sirik overlooking the Strait of Hormuz, though US Central Command said it intercepted two Iranian drones. While Iran’s Assembly of Experts urged a nuclear doctrine review, Trump disclosed that Saudi Arabia asked him to hold back from major strikes and that he told Vice-President JD Vance to drop Iran peace diplomacy. A YouGov poll found 65% of Britons and 79% of 2024 Labour voters oppose resuming the war, with 54% against US strikes from UK bases, even as US Air Force crews responded to suspected drones over RAF Lakenheath on Friday night. In Israel, prime ministerial designate Gadi Eisenkot accused Benjamin Netanyahu and Itamar Ben Gvir of waging a racist campaign against Arab Israeli voters and MPs. (Guardian, Guardian, BBC, Guardian)

Met Police open criminal inquiry into David Walliams as probation officers vote for industrial action and No 10 weighs wider benefit reforms

Metropolitan Police detectives from the complex sexual offences unit have opened a criminal investigation into comedian and children’s author David Walliams after several people came forward this week alleging non-recent serious sexual offences dating back to the 2000s. Led by Detective Superintendent Mike Cagney, the inquiry examines complaints separate from the grooming and harassment claims published earlier this week after Walliams lost a High Court bid to block coverage, as bookshops and parents clear his books from shelves. Walliams, 55, who is in a medical facility and has not been arrested, denies breaking the law. Meanwhile, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has sent rules for cabinet approval ahead of a December vote extending Britain’s under-16s social media ban to Depop, eBay and Facebook Marketplace—and enforcing age checks on Vinted—after warnings that predators use them to solicit children’s worn underwear and scrape photos for AI deepfakes. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian)

Across the justice system, probation union Napo voted by up to 87% for overtime bans from 23 November and up to 75% for strikes after rejecting a 5% pay offer and protesting over caseloads swollen by prison early releases. Around 2,000 inmates have been freed since 1 October—rising to 2,500 by year-end, with nine further cohorts including prisoners serving over 12 years due out by June—even after inspectors found nearly half of electronic tags were fitted late. In Whitehall, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden are weighing whether to expand Alan Milburn’s “participation first” overhaul of under-25 disability benefits to claimants over 25 alongside the Stephen Timms PIP review, despite clashes over drawing £6bn in training funds from health and education budgets. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian)

In Westminster, Reform UK spent over £150,000 from party funds in the past year on a security team and two cars for Nigel Farage after he refused a Home Office bodyguard, prompting Labour and the Conservatives to question Farage’s claim that Christopher Harborne’s £5m gift was for his personal security. Ahead of Burnham’s 20 November UK-EU summit, Lord Gove and Oliver Lewis launched the Stay Out campaign, claiming EU re-entry would cost £39.3bn a year. In the courts, Eleanor Donaldson, 60, wife of jailed ex-DUP leader Jeffrey Donaldson, was placed on the sex offender register for five years for aiding his child sex offences; and former Hamas bodyguard Mohammed Alfatih, 40, was convicted of a Birmingham knife attack while awaiting extradition to Germany over a plot against Israelis. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian)

Brazilian Senate approves fiscal adjustment package as rejected police report links Supreme Court justices to Banco Master owner

Brazil’s Senate approved the base text of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s fiscal adjustment bill by 45 votes to 31, backing measures projected by Planning Minister Bruno Moretti to save R$46bn to R$56bn (£6.2bn–£7.5bn) in 2027 before Tuesday’s vote on amendments and transfer to the Chamber of Deputies. Two-thirds of the adjustment—R$33bn to R$38.3bn—comes from curbing tax breaks and corporate tax credit offsets, which São Paulo industry leader Paulo Skaf called a R$40bn tax hike. While the economic team prepares a constitutional amendment to cut R$20bn from mandatory spending including the Fundeb education fund and Federal District fund, Workers’ Party leader Lindbergh Farias is drafting an alternative to tax banks, large fortunes and LCI and LCA bonds. (Meio, Meio, Folha)

Meanwhile, the crisis at the Federal Police (PF) and Supreme Federal Court (STF) deepened after details emerged from the report on Banco Master owner Daniel Vorcaro that PF leadership rejected before dismissing anti-corruption chiefs Daniel Mostardeiro Cola and Wedson Cajé Lopes. Phone messages show Vorcaro told associates in February 2024—three months before a May ruling—that justices Alexandre de Moraes and Kassio Nunes Marques would vote for his interests in a constitutional case (ADC 81) on opening private medical courses, where Vorcaro was a creditor to the Lutheran University of Brazil via Fundo Calêndula; Nunes Marques denied communicating with or voting for Vorcaro, while Moraes did not comment. A 2 October dispatch showed PF chief Andrei Rodrigues had forwarded STF President Edson Fachin’s request for findings before sacking the delegates, prompting the PF delegates’ union to call Rodrigues’s position unsustainable as Fachin and Justice Gilmar Mendes moved to bar police and military officers from STF chambers. (Folha, Folha, Meio)

Elsewhere in Brazil’s courts, Federal Judge João Paulo Pirôpo de Abreu ordered the government to invest R$597m (£80m) in Canudos, Bahia, as reparations for the Army’s 1896–97 massacre of Antônio Conselheiro’s community and the 1969 flooding of its ruins. Speaking in Rio de Janeiro, Fachin urged Lula to fill the Supreme Court seat vacated by Luís Roberto Barroso—after the Senate rejected attorney-general Jorge Messias—with the first Black woman in the court’s 135-year history. Electoral Court Justice Dias Toffoli also gave Lula’s campaign three days to explain subcontractor and travel records, while STF Justice Flávio Dino allowed companies to spread the new 42-hour workweek across five shifts of eight hours and 24 minutes without overtime pay during the transition starting on 16 December. (Folha, Folha, Folha, Meio)

Economy

Disclosures reveal Trump bought millions in Nvidia stock while loosening China chip rules as cabinet feud erupts over Megaspeed

Public financial disclosures show that Donald Trump bought millions of dollars in Nvidia stock immediately before and after his administration dismantled export restrictions on selling advanced AI chips to China. Following Jensen Huang’s resignation as Nvidia chief executive on Thursday and the appointment of chief financial officer Colette Kress as interim head, anti-corruption group DeKleptocracy found that Trump bought $1m to $5m (£760,000–£3.8m) of Nvidia shares in May 2025 days before rescinding a Biden-era rule restricting AI chip exports to Beijing. After Trump announced in December 2025 that Nvidia could sell H200 processors to China—approved in January 2026 despite warnings that the chips were six times faster than Chinese alternatives—he made at least three more Nvidia share purchases of $250,001 to $500,000 each. (Guardian, The Verge)

The fallout has sparked cabinet infighting, with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent blaming Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Friday for failing to blacklist Megaspeed, the Singaporean data centre firm run by Huang’s former partner and suspected Chinese operative Alice Huang. Bessent noted ahead of Lutnick’s Senate testimony next month that US agencies had pushed for months to blacklist Megaspeed to halt chip leakages above the H100 threshold. In Singapore—which accounted for nearly a fifth of Nvidia’s billing last year although under 1% of those chips physically entered the country—authorities confirmed investigating Megaspeed since February 2025 over suspected false export declarations. Greenpeace also urged Kress to curb Nvidia’s supply-chain emissions, up 725% since 2020 to 10.7m metric tons of CO2, with chip electricity use generating 21m metric tons annually. (BBC, BBC, The Verge)

IEA declares ‘age of electricity’ at Cop31 as Jaguar Land Rover posts £451m loss and UK insurers face climate subsidence surge

The world has left fossil fuel dominance behind and entered the “age of electricity”, International Energy Agency chief Fatih Birol declared on Friday at the Cop31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey. Driven by a 60% jump in electric car sales outside China over the past nine months, AI datacentres and surging air-conditioning demand, global power capacity is set to grow by 12,000 gigawatts over the next decade—more than double the 5,000GW added in the past ten years—as 185 nations debate a target of deriving 35% of final energy from electricity by 2035 despite Saudi and Russian opposition. As world leaders departed Antalya, outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres used his farewell Cop speech before stepping down in December to warn that peace and poverty reduction are impossible on a burning planet. (Guardian, Guardian)

In UK manufacturing, Jaguar Land Rover reported a £451m quarterly loss after £530m in restructuring charges to cut 4,000 jobs, even as revenues rose to £5.9bn. Chief executive PB Balaji urged the UK and EU to scrap 10% “rules of origin” tariffs due on 1 January to counter Chinese EV competition as JLR rolls out its electric Range Rover and finalises a US manufacturing deal with Stellantis. Meanwhile, insurers Aviva, Axa and Hastings Direct—where claims jumped 140% in August—reported a surge in domestic subsidence claims averaging a record £20,000 after two record-hot summers shrank clay soils beneath foundations, with the British Geological Survey warning 4.2 million UK homes face subsidence risk by 2070. (Guardian, Guardian)

In regional finance, unions and employers in Bournemouth—where 2,500 firms employing 24,000 staff, led by JP Morgan’s 5,300-worker campus processing $1tn (£750bn) daily, provide 10% of Dorset’s output—warned that banks are cutting entry-level and compliance roles after 5,000 AI-linked cuts at Barclays and 7,000 at Standard Chartered. Elsewhere, all 197 people aboard survived when the tanker Atlantic Asphalt lost steering on the Mississippi River in New Orleans and T-boned the cruise ship American Heritage, hospitalising 32 with minor injuries; the US Supreme Court agreed to review Trump’s border asylum ban; and Hungary seized $19.5m (£14.8m) in cash buried in forests and safes during a graft probe into former minister Miklós Seszták. (Guardian, Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian)

Technology

AI decodes hundreds of lost theorems in Kurt Gödel’s shorthand notebooks as SpaceX launches Starship Flight 15 and OpenAI rolls out agent wallet

Researchers at Helsinki University have used Anthropic’s Claude AI to unlock hundreds of previously unknown proved theorems inside 16 unpublished notebooks written in the early 1940s by Austrian logician Kurt Gödel, whose 1931 incompleteness theorems laid the foundations of modern computing. Led since 2017 by Finnish logician Jan von Plato under a €2.5m (£2.1m) European Research Council grant, the team spent years transcribing Gödel’s 1,009 pages of obsolete Gabelsberger German shorthand at a page a week before feeding them into Claude, which produced a 650-page digest in days revealing 14 unexplored themes and results anticipating discoveries from the 1970s and 1980s. In Texas, SpaceX launched its 407ft (124m) Starship on Flight 15 to deploy 26 Starlink satellites over 14 orbits, though it aborted the first half of a double-catch test when the Super Heavy booster splashed down in the Gulf of Mexico ahead of Saturday’s upper-stage catch attempt. (Guardian, Guardian, BBC)

Across the AI sector, OpenAI launched ChatGPT Wallet for US Pro subscribers holding Amex, Chase, Mastercard or Visa cards, using biometric checks and tokenised credentials so its “Dots” agents can buy items online without exposing card numbers. Rival Amazon is building a “World Product Graph” slated for October 2027 to index every product sold online, aiming to keep shoppers and AI bots on its site while fixing errors in Alexa for Shopping. Meanwhile, Google released Gemini 4 Hydrogen—running 2.5 times faster than Gemini 3.8 Flash at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens alongside Carbon and Argon in Antigravity—while Anthropic added Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, Google Meet note-taker Claude Meetings, and connectors for Adobe, Atlassian and Box. (The Verge, 9to5Mac, The Verge, MacMagazine, MacMagazine)

Apple began deliveries on Friday for its $299 HomeView smart display—a 7-inch Siri AI hub with an A18 chip, 12MP camera, Face ID profile switching and a 0.3-nit display—alongside the $299 A19-powered Apple TV 4K and the first LG and Schneider doorbell and cameras in the Apple Home Collection. Early Apple TV 4K buyers hit a YouTube app block fixed by installing tvOS 27.2.1—which also brings Siri AI to older Apple TV 4K models—and reinstalling the app, while filings showed Apple preparing to launch the HomePod mini 2 in Brazil. In Washington, Epic Games filed its Supreme Court response urging justices to uphold the contempt ruling against Apple over its 27% fee on external payment links. (9to5Mac, MacStories, 9to5Mac, The Verge, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac)

Grand Theft Auto VI’s 212GB pre-load exposes UK broadband blackspots as Robert Pattinson leads James Bond race and Ireland unseals banned books

Ahead of Rockstar Games’ release of Grand Theft Auto VI next Friday, 19 November, after a 13-year wait, a Broadband Genie study of 17,000 speed tests warned that 870,000 UK gamers on connections of 2.8Mbps or slower face download waits of over a week for its 212GB pre-load on PS5 and Xbox, led by Newport where 35% of tests fell below that mark. Rockstar has guarded the game—which pairs protagonists Jason and Lucia, runs at 30fps and includes an in-game animated TV series—so closely that original 1997 GTA co-creator Dave Jones and writer Brian Baglow confirmed in Dundee they are waiting on standard pre-orders. Elsewhere, Sony rolled out Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR) AI upscaling on base PS5 consoles for Marvel’s Spider-Man 2, with updates following for Arc Raiders, The Finals, No Man’s Sky, Control Resonant and Hell Let Loose: Vietnam. (IGN, BBC, IGN, IGN)

In film and literature, Robert Pattinson has emerged as Amazon MGM’s frontrunner ahead of Nicholas Hoult, Callum Turner, Jack Lowden and Josh O’Connor to succeed Daniel Craig in the 26th James Bond film—directed by Denis Villeneuve and written by Steven Knight—under a reported three-film deal, while an original Darth Vader lightsaber prop sold at auction for nearly $5m. In Dublin, Ireland’s Department of Justice is moving 12,000 books from its closed “banned books room”—outlawed between 1926 and 1996, including works by Edna O’Brien, Oscar Wilde, Brendan Behan, DH Lawrence, Ian Fleming and Iris Murdoch—alongside censors’ ledgers to the National Archives. Tributes were also paid to British-born journalist and author Simon Winchester, who died aged 82 after reporting on Bloody Sunday, Watergate and the Falklands and writing 30 books including The Surgeon of Crowthorne. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Sports

Tearful Mauricio Pochettino leaves US national team for Manchester United as Crystal Palace sack Pierre Sage and Arsenal hold Barcelona

Mauricio Pochettino broke down in tears at US Soccer’s training centre on Friday after Manchester United paid roughly $10m (£7.5m) in compensation to appoint him as Michael Carrick’s successor until June 2029. Although Pochettino signed an extension in August to lead the US through the 2030 World Cup—with part of his $6m salary funded by billionaire Ken Griffin—he said United first made contact on Sunday with an offer too difficult to refuse. He will coach the US in Saturday and Tuesday’s Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals against Haiti before starting at Old Trafford on 18 November, where former Spurs defender Toby Alderweireld warned players to expect a fitness-obsessed “control freak”. Elsewhere in the Premier League, Crystal Palace sacked French manager Pierre Sage in an 83-word statement six months after hiring him, with Palace averaging 43.2% possession and sitting bottom for goals from high turnovers. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian)

In the Women’s Champions League, Arsenal earned a 1-1 draw against reigning European champions Barcelona at the Camp Nou on Thursday night in a match delayed by 24 hours because of Wednesday’s general strike in Spain. Playing in the No 10 role behind Alessia Russo—who has 12 goals in nine games for club and country—Frida Maanum put Arsenal ahead in the first half after Russo beat two defenders on the left and crossed for Caitlin Foord, whose shot was parried by Cata Coll into Maanum’s path. Caroline Graham Hansen equalised after half-time, but Renée Slegers’s low block held firm before 1,000 travelling fans to keep Arsenal fourth in the Champions League table and inflict a rare home draw on the Spanish champions. (Guardian)

The Fold

A daily briefing for Londoners who want the full picture in one place.

item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 12 November 2026: Nvidia's board meets to decide Jensen Huang's future as its market value drops by $600bn, UK ministers warn the entertainment industry to strengthen safeguarding or face mandatory rules, Russia and Ukraine agree a record prisoner swap in Abu Dhabi, and Democrat Scott Colom wins a historic US Senate seat in Mississippi.
item.content:encoded:
Thursday 12 November 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • Nvidia’s board convenes to decide whether to oust co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang after revelations of a second workplace affair compound a Chinese espionage investigation and wipe $600bn off the chipmaker’s value.
  • Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy warns television, film and publishing bosses to strengthen safeguarding or face mandatory regulation after the David Walliams and Russell Brand scandals, while Alan Milburn’s welfare review proposes moving under-25s off main sickness benefits.
  • Russia and Ukraine agree to the largest prisoner exchange of the war at US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi, Democrat Scott Colom wins a historic Senate upset in Mississippi, and Spain’s first general strike in 14 years paralyses major cities over housing costs.
  • Climate Action Tracker warns at Cop31 that current policies will heat the planet by 2.7C as satellite data reveals 500 oil spills from the US-Iran war in the Gulf and Andy Burnham hails a £12.8bn Norfolk offshore wind deal.
  • Brazil’s government negotiates an R$80bn fiscal adjustment touching constitutional health and education floors as Senate committees summon the Justice Minister and Federal Police chief over the Banco Master crisis.
  • Manchester United reach a framework agreement with Mauricio Pochettino to replace Michael Carrick as Harry Kane breaks Peter Shilton’s England appearance record and an IRS complaint challenges Gianni Infantino’s domestic staffing at Fifa.

News

Nvidia board meets to decide Jensen Huang’s future as second affair allegation and espionage crisis wipe $600bn off chipmaker

Nvidia’s board of directors is convening to decide whether to dismiss co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang after disclosures of a second extramarital affair—this time with a subordinate executive—sharply escalated a crisis triggered by his relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence operative. The latest allegation centres on Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice-president of healthcare, who reports directly to Huang and was allegedly filmed with him at a San Jose hotel during March’s GTC developer conference. On Sunday Huang sent a memo to staff admitting marital infidelity after revelations of his affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, a Chinese businesswoman whom US intelligence believes helped facilitate shipments of advanced Nvidia chips to China. Although an independent board committee hired former acting Manhattan US attorney Joon Kim of Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz on Tuesday to lead an internal inquiry while stating that Huang would continue running the company without interruption, directors are now preparing to act before that probe concludes. (Guardian, Guardian, The Verge)

Shares in the $4tn (£3tn) chipmaker tumbled 8% in after-hours trading on Wednesday, erasing a daytime rebound lifted by strong results at AI cloud provider CoreWeave and bringing Nvidia’s market value loss since Friday to roughly $600bn. Under company bylaws, Huang, 63, who owns 3.6% of Nvidia and holds a personal fortune near $150bn, can be removed with or without cause by a simple board majority. His departure would leave an immediate vacuum at the centre of the global AI buildout: US tech giants plan to spend $750bn on AI infrastructure this year, much of it on Nvidia’s datacentre hardware, which grew 92% year on year in May to $75.2bn, and Huang oversees dozens of direct reports without an anointed successor. (Guardian, Guardian)

In Washington, Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons wrote to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller demanding the preservation of all records relating to Nvidia’s China export licences and Huang’s ties to Alice Huang. House Republican chairs John Moolenaar, Brian Mast and Rick Crawford warned that Huang faces subpoenas unless he agrees to a closed-door briefing on whether Beijing accessed privileged technology. The scandal has also complicated Donald Trump’s alliance with Huang, who lobbied for looser export rules, joined Trump’s delegation to meet Xi Jinping in Beijing in May and received the National Medal of Science in October; Trump said earlier this week that the FBI was investigating and that he believed Huang never knew Alice Huang was a spy. (Guardian)

Ministers threaten statutory crackdown on entertainment industry over Walliams and Brand as Milburn review targets under-25 sickness benefits

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy will summon television, film and publishing executives to a roundtable next week to warn that ministers will legislate to compel participation in the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority (CIISA) unless the sector strengthens safeguards for women, children and whistleblowers. The warning follows Monday’s ten-and-a-half-year rape sentence for Russell Brand and allegations that comedian and children’s author David Walliams groomed teenage fans as young as 15 and harassed junior staff. Equalities Minister Bridget Phillipson, Justice Secretary Alex Norris, Commons committee chair Olivia Bailey and campaigner Zelda Perkins called for tighter curbs on non-disclosure agreements and privacy injunctions covering freelancers, volunteers and fans. Walliams—who denies breaking the law or acting as a sexual predator while admitting he sometimes behaved thoughtlessly in casual relationships—has had his cameo cut from the Australian film adaptation of his 2019 book Fing!, dropped by Sky in the UK and Stan in Australia, while Thames Valley Police confirmed officers removed Brand from ex-girlfriend Jemima Goldsmith’s Oxfordshire home in July 2014 after a reported violent incident. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, BBC)

In welfare policy, former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn will publish a review on Tuesday proposing that claimants under 25 be removed from the health element of universal credit and personal independence payment and placed on basic universal credit, alongside a targeted cost allowance, higher severe-disability payments and billions for job placements and wage subsidies. Backed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham to cut the nearly one million 18- to 24-year-olds out of education, work or training, the overhaul will be legislated in the new year with penalties for refusing support. Meanwhile, Lord Cameron warned that Burnham’s openness to rejoining the EU risked weakening Britain’s hand ahead of Thursday’s Dublin talks and next week’s Brussels summit; Reform UK general secretary Tom Waterhouse resigned after Hampshire council leader George Madgwick was charged with 12 counts of rape; Phillipson criticised Kemi Badenoch for dropping Tory support for banning conversion practices; and a Wigan inquiry heard Burnham warned before entering No 10 that lorries at Whistl’s Astley warehouse endangered schoolchildren. (BBC, BBC, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Across policing, His Majesty’s Inspectorate of Constabulary warned that officers have treated biased retrospective facial recognition matches as evidence without corroboration, putting ethnic minorities at risk of wrongful arrest while forces unlawfully keep custody photos. On Wednesday, 1,000 schools in Scotland, 300 in Northern Ireland and 6,000 in Italy received hoax bomb emails, while L/Cpl Nicholas Horne was remanded for court martial charged with raping a servicewoman in Cyprus, and Prestwick DJ James Campbell, 32, was named as the Briton killed in Saturday’s Kraków shooting. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Russia and Ukraine agree record prisoner swap in Abu Dhabi as Democrat Scott Colom wins Mississippi Senate upset and strike halts Spain

Russia and Ukraine have agreed to the largest prisoner exchange of the war—freeing more than 1,000 captives on each side—after US-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi led by Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who meet Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Thursday before briefing Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Dublin. Speaking alongside Irish Taoiseach Micheál Martin, Zelenskyy saw a window for peace before 2027 if US envoys returned with specifics, while Ukrainian delegate Davyd Arakhamia noted progress on security guarantees. Russian negotiator Vladimir Medinsky insisted Moscow would accept peace only on its own terms, demanded Ukrainian-held Donetsk, dismissed European envoys as hotel tourists, and called for a new Yalta and Potsdam, as Russian strikes killed three people in Odesa and Ukrainian drones hit five fuel tanks at Russia’s Baltic port of Ust-Luga. (Guardian, Guardian, BBC)

In the United States, Democrat Scott Colom unseated Republican Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith in Mississippi after a week of counting across 82 counties, becoming the state’s first Black US senator since Reconstruction in 1875, its first popularly elected Black senator, and its first Democratic senator since 1982. A former district attorney whose federal judgeship nomination by Joe Biden was blocked by Hyde-Smith, Colom campaigned at barber shops, Waffle Houses and a Donald Trump rally in Corinth, turning cattle rancher Hyde-Smith’s remark that voters worried about beef prices had “so many proteins to choose from” into a viral burger advert and taco truck tour that lifted the Democratic Senate majority to at least 55 seats. Off Destin, Florida, the retired liner SS United States was sunk on Wednesday night to form the world’s largest artificial reef. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Across Spain, millions joined the country’s first general strike in 14 years on Wednesday over a housing crisis that pushed rents up 80% and home prices up 63% in a decade, putting an average 50-square-metre Madrid flat at €1,170 (£1,000) a month—nearly half the €2,460 average gross wage—following the eviction and death of 87-year-old tenant Maricarmen Abascal. Backed by tenants’ groups and the CCOO and UGT unions, the stoppage reached 90% in ports and car plants, blocked Barcelona’s AP-7 motorway and drew 120,000 marchers in Madrid before clashes in Barcelona. Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, facing a 29 November snap election after rightwing parties defeated his housing bill, praised union gains, whereas opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo and Madrid president Isabel Díaz Ayuso called the unions a “mafia”. (Guardian, BBC)

Climate Action Tracker warns of 2.7C warming overshoot and Gulf war oil slicks spread as Burnham hails £12bn Norfolk wind deal

The world faces an irrecoverable overshoot of the 1.5C Paris limit, with current policies projected to heat the planet by 2.7C by 2100—up from 2.6C last year—and full delivery of national pledges still yielding 1.9C, Climate Action Tracker warned on Thursday at Cop31 in Antalya. Although high fossil fuel prices from the Iran war and clean energy investment double that of fossil fuels are projected by Nature Climate Change to trim global emissions by 0.4% in 2026, developing nations face delays because major donors including France, Germany and Cop31 co-host Australia have yet to set post-2026 finance commitments toward the $300bn-a-year goal for 2035. Meanwhile, satellite analysis by Greenpeace and Pax mapped over 500 oil spills covering 20,000 square kilometres—nearly the size of Wales—across the Strait of Hormuz, Persian Gulf and Arabian Sea since the US-Iran conflict began on 28 February, after 133 tanker attacks and strikes on Lavan Island storage tanks. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Meio)

Ahead of speaking at Cop31, Andy Burnham hailed a £12.8bn financing deal led by RWE and KKR to build the 2.8-gigawatt Vanguard West and East windfarms off Norfolk—powering three million homes by 2030 and supporting 2,300 jobs—alongside SSE’s Berwick Bank B in Scotland. Seeking to repair its green record after approving the Jackdaw gasfield and rejecting the £800m Botley West solar farm, the government committed a £1bn National Wealth Fund loan despite developers holding a 20-year contract at £91.20 per megawatt hour. Meanwhile, Labour’s climate caucus urged Deputy Prime Minister Louise Haigh against cutting the 2030 electric vehicle mandate from 80% to 60%–65%; Environment Agency data showed banned PFOS and PFOA chemicals in English rivers fell 30% and 29% over a decade; England and Scotland ordered flocks of 50 or more birds indoors against avian flu; and Argentina told the maritime tribunal in Hamburg ahead of a 28 November ruling that UK oil drilling at the Falklands’ Sea Lion field echoed 17th-century imperial claims. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian)

Brazil negotiates R$80bn fiscal package touching health and education floors as Senate summons PF chief over Banco Master and Harvard returns skulls

Finance Minister Dario Durigan and Senate President Davi Alcolumbre are negotiating an R$80bn (£11bn) fiscal adjustment for 2027—0.5% of GDP—authorised by President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva before departing for Cop31 in Turkey and ASEAN talks in Manila provided campaign pledges remain untouched. Tabled this week as a complementary bill ahead of a wider 2027–30 package, the plan removes extraordinary oil and gas revenues from Brazil’s constitutional floors of 15% of net current revenue for health and 18% of tax revenue for education, while Central Bank chief Gabriel Galípolo warned against artificial rate caps. In Congress, lawmakers filed 179 amendments to exempt diet soda, pickup trucks, draught beer, speedboats, ride-hailing cars and communion wine from the “sin tax”, and business groups lobbied Alcolumbre over ending the 6x1 work week after Justice Flávio Dino confirmed the 40-hour limit starts in December 2027. After a study showed R$61bn in budget amendments failed to stop Centrão parties losing 20 Chamber seats to Jair Bolsonaro’s PL, União Brasil and PP backed Alcolumbre’s February re-election in exchange for ministries and burying a parliamentary inquiry into Banco Master, though Alcolumbre faced criticism over a R$6m Senate tender to lease 95 iPhone 18 Pro handsets and 330 other phones. (Meio, Meio, Folha, Folha, Folha)

The Banco Master crisis deepened on Wednesday as two Senate committees invited Justice Minister Wellington Lima e Silva, Federal Police chief Andrei Rodrigues and removed anti-corruption coordinators Daniel Mostardeiro Cola and Wedson Cajé Lopes to a joint hearing on 18 November. Although Supreme Court dean Gilmar Mendes defended Rodrigues after the PF chief ordered officers to strip value judgments from reports on jailed banker Daniel Vorcaro’s ties to six justices, officials view Rodrigues’s position as fragile ahead of creating a Public Security Ministry. Elsewhere, Dino ordered a PF inquiry into suspected foreign funding of Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign via Meta and the US Rockbridge Network; a Quaest poll found 62% of voters feel unrepresented by any party; São Paulo Governor Tarcísio de Freitas named five former Bolsonaro officials including Ricardo Salles to his cabinet; and Brazil repatriated two 19th-century skulls of enslaved Afro-Brazilians from Harvard’s Peabody Museum—including a suspected rebel from Salvador’s 1835 Malê uprising and a young woman exhumed in Rio during Louis Agassiz’s expedition—for burial. (Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha, Folha, Guardian)

Economy

MPs accuse Poundland owner of asset-stripping ahead of High Court rescue hearing as UK diesel stays near £2 and Nissan cuts petrol output

Poundland’s management goes to the High Court on Thursday seeking a ten-working-day extension to creditor protection for the 600-store chain and its 12,000 staff after US distressed-investment firm Gordon Brothers released £19m from £50m in frozen company cash to restock for Christmas. After grilling Gordon Brothers European head Mark Newton-Jones on Wednesday, Commons business committee chair Liam Byrne accused the firm—which bought Poundland from Pepco for £1 in June 2025—of acting like a “wolf on Wall Street, on the British High Street” by extracting millions while starving the retailer of its own cash and rejecting three whole-company rescue bids from buyers including Martin Property Group and Xyra Group to profit from selling store parcels to Tesco, B&M and Poundstretcher, despite chief executive Barry Williams delivering an £18.1m annual profit and an 11.4% sales rise. (Guardian, BBC)

In transport and manufacturing, UK unleaded petrol has fallen 6p from October’s peak to 168p a litre—with the AA forecasting another 10p drop after wholesale costs dipped below 62p—yet diesel remains at 197p as Federal Reserve governor Christopher Waller told a London conference that Strait of Hormuz war-risk insurance, ship-to-ship transfers and tight refining capacity are adding $20 to $30 a barrel to oil. High pump prices helped lift UK used electric car sales by 56% year on year in October to a 10% market share on Autotrader, while Nissan cut its annual global sales forecast to between 2.97 million and 3 million vehicles and scaled back petrol production after China’s EV price war cut its nine-month Chinese sales by 32%, with chief executive Ivan Espinosa urging Brussels to include Sunderland-built cars in “Made in Europe” rules. (Guardian, Guardian)

Technology

Brussels proposes Digital Fairness Act targeting loot boxes and dark patterns as researchers flag unpatched iOS flaw and DeepMind unveils AlphaGenome 2

The European Commission unveiled its draft Digital Fairness Act on Wednesday, proposing fines of up to 6% of global turnover to ban manipulative dark patterns, addictive “rabbit-hole” social media feeds, relentless notifications, undisclosed influencer promotions, hidden pricing and video game loot boxes or virtual currencies sold to children—measures EU Commissioner Michael McGrath estimated will save consumers €13.7bn ($15.1bn) annually. In mobile security, crypto exchange Binance urged iPhone users to delete sideloaded apps after researchers @0xjohnny and @forcequitOS published a proof of concept for worse_query, an unpatched flaw in iOS 26.7.1 through iOS 27.3 beta 1 that bypasses the iOS sandbox so malicious apps can read local files from other apps, including crypto keys and WhatsApp data. Meanwhile, Apple met Thai Digital Economy Minister Chaichanok Chidchob after mercenary spyware alerts across 99 countries hit Thai politicians, and Cupertino police arrested Apple employee Eric Chen Su on vehicular manslaughter charges after a 150km/h crash beside Apple Park killed a nanny and a two-year-old child. (The Verge, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine)

Across Apple’s ecosystem, iOS 27.3 beta adds a Global Privacy Control toggle in Safari to reject cookie banners alongside vertical tabs, iOS 27 brings Apple Intelligence video summaries and search to HomeKit Secure Video on 2TB-plus iCloud+ tiers, CNET’s 32-phone battery test crowned the iPhone 18 Pro Max and foldable iPhone Duo ahead of the Pixel 11 Pro XL, smoke tests by Geekerwan showed the touchscreen PROLED XDR MacBook Pro vents heat through its hinge in clamshell mode, and Chinese supplier Quick Intelligent Equipment pointed to camera-equipped AirPods and Apple smart glasses. In AI, Google brought hands-free Gemini Live to Apple CarPlay and unveiled DeepMind’s AlphaGenome 2—trained on 100 million single-cell profiles across 68 tissues to double detection of disease-linked gene variants—while Anthropic launched Claude Meetings, Whiteboards and Sheets, OpenAI released ChatGPT Finances for macOS, Brazil barred unsupervised school AI up to fifth grade, and United Airlines blocked third-party bots such as OpenAI’s Dots and Meta’s Muse from booking flights because agents cannot legally certify baggage safety. (9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac, The Verge, The Verge)

CD Projekt Red uses AI to restore stroke-hit Polish Geralt actor’s voice for Witcher 3 expansion as Nintendo defends cutting Mario cameos from Ocarina of Time

CD Projekt Red confirmed it is using Respeecher synthetic voice technology—with the full consent of Polish actor Jacek Rozenek—to restore Rozenek’s 2014 vocal tone as Geralt of Rivia in Songs of the Past, a new expansion for The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt arriving 11 years after the original game. After a 2019 stroke temporarily left Rozenek unable to speak and left his recovered voice deeper and easily fatigued, audio engineers trained a model on his 2014 lines so his newly recorded dialogue matches the original era, while localization producer Mikołaj Szwed said Rozenek’s natural older voice will be used for an aged Geralt in The Witcher 4. Elsewhere, Nintendo announced its Switch 2 remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time has sold 5.2 million copies since 5 November—with players using its microphone ocarina mode to summon Epona by mimicking Family Guy’s Lois Griffin—as producers Eiji Aonuma and Hidemaro Fujibayashi defended cutting the 1998 original’s Hyrule Castle Mario portraits to preserve immersion, and insiders reported Skydance’s Marvel 1943: Rise of Hydra is nearing completion after cuts to length and interactivity. (IGN, IGN, IGN, IGN)

Culture

Gilded Roman bronze leg goes on display in Edinburgh as councils keep 95% of public art in storage and Coachella unveils 2027 lineup

A gilded bronze leg dug out of a Dumfriesshire bog in 1820 and kept for a century in the Duke of Buccleuch’s charter room goes on display on Saturday in Roman Scotland: Life on the Edge of Empire at the National Museum of Scotland in Edinburgh. Once dismissed as loot hacked from York by northern tribes, the “Mislington leg” is now identified by curator Dr Fraser Hunter as part of an equestrian statue of Emperor Antoninus Pius erected near Hawick around AD140, shown alongside two painted Mithras altars and a cavalry horse skeleton from Inveresk. Meanwhile, freedom-of-information requests across 225 English councils revealed local authorities hold more than 500,000 artworks—including works by David Hockney, Tracey Emin, LS Lowry and Antony Gormley—yet display only 26,856 (5%), with Rugby Borough Council the sole authority with over 100 works exhibiting all 257 while Kent and Derbyshire sold hundreds after shutting storage services. (Guardian, BBC)

In music and film, Coachella announced its April 2027 lineup in Indio, California, with Dua Lipa becoming the first British female solo headliner alongside SZA and Tame Impala, while Madonna returns to headline the dance tent 21 years after her 2006 appearance following her chart-topping album Confessions II, joined by Phoebe Bridgers, Robyn, Jorja Smith, Underworld and Lambrini Girls, and Paul McCartney and Ringo Starr set a January 2027 VetsAid reunion in Las Vegas. Tributes were also paid to founding Television guitarist Richard Lloyd, whose interplay with Tom Verlaine at CBGB and on 1977’s Marquee Moon shaped post-punk before his death from cancer aged 75, and former Texas teacher Irma P Hall, who won a Cannes jury prize in the Coen brothers’ The Ladykillers and an NAACP Image Award in Soul Food before dying aged 91. (Guardian, Meio, Guardian, Guardian)

Manchester United agree Pochettino framework ahead of Carrick decision as Kane breaks England cap record and IRS receives Infantino complaint

Manchester United have agreed a contract framework with United States coach Mauricio Pochettino to replace Michael Carrick, whose dismissal after one win in ten Premier League matches—leaving United 18th, their lowest position at this stage since 1986-87—follows Wednesday’s Monaco talks between Sir Jim Ratcliffe, chief executive Omar Berrada and football director Jason Wilcox and a board vote with the Glazer family. Pochettino, 54, is set to join on a fourth approach after United pay his $10m (£7.5m) US Soccer release clause ahead of visiting Liverpool on 22 November, when Marcus Rashford targets a return from injury. England manager Thomas Tuchel confirmed ahead of Thursday’s Nations League match against Croatia at Wembley that his contract through Euro 2028 contains no release clause, citing “unfinished business” after June’s World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina as Dan Burn, Jarell Quansah and Arsenal’s Declan Rice start alongside captain Harry Kane, who receives a presentation from Peter Shilton on winning his record 126th men’s cap two weeks after claiming the Ballon d’Or. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian, Guardian)

In football governance, Washington lawyer Abed Ayoub filed a US Internal Revenue Service complaint alleging an employee paid by a Fifa-linked entity worked solely as a private housekeeper for Fifa president Gianni Infantino at his Miami home—a claim Fifa denied, saying Infantino pays domestic staff personally—as incoming House Judiciary chair Jamie Raskin scrutinises Fifa’s tax-exempt status and former president Sepp Blatter called Infantino a “dictator” in Der Spiegel for awarding Donald Trump a Fifa peace prize before the Iran war. Meanwhile, US Soccer withdrew from next week’s Under-17 World Cup in Qatar over Gulf conflict risks; Fifa confirmed the top four seeds (Spain, the US, Germany and England) will be kept apart until the semi-finals at the 2027 Women’s World Cup in Brazil while approving the 2031 US-led and 2035 UK bids; and tributes were paid to Football365 co-founder, former NME editor and TalkSport host Danny Kelly, who died of oesophageal cancer aged 69. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

The Fold

A daily briefing for Londoners who want the full picture in one place.

Inspired by Brazil’s Meio · Thursday, 12 November 2026 · leonardoresston.github.io/thefold

item.title: The Fold — 2026-11-11
item.description: The Fold morning briefing for 11 November 2026: UK counter-terrorism police arrest a senior US soldier over alleged Russian spying, David Walliams is accused of preying on young women after losing a High Court anonymity bid, a US judge lets Donald Trump's $10bn BBC lawsuit proceed, and Anthropic trims its IPO valuation target to $1.4tn.
item.content:encoded:
Wednesday 11 November 2026 · London

The Fold

Your morning briefing from the UK & the world

In this edition

  • British counter-terrorism police arrest a senior US Army soldier in Gloucestershire on suspicion of spying for Russia while US prosecutors indict an Iranian cell over the RAF Fairford bomb plot.
  • Comedian and children’s author David Walliams is accused by multiple women of grooming teenage fans and abusing his celebrity status after the High Court rejects his bid for a permanent anonymity injunction.
  • A federal judge in Florida allows Donald Trump’s $10bn defamation lawsuit against the BBC to proceed while House Republicans block a move to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth.
  • Labour MPs warn that Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s 10-year strategy lacks industrial firepower as Baroness Louise Casey warns that nobody is in charge of England’s chaotic social care system.
  • A rift inside Brazil’s Federal Police deepens after two commissioners investigating Banco Master and Supreme Court justices are removed from their posts, while the electoral court fines Meta R$7.5m.
  • Anthropic trims its Wall Street flotation target to $1.4tn amid investor caution over artificial intelligence infrastructure costs, while Nvidia hires Wachtell Lipton to investigate Jensen Huang.

News

UK police arrest senior US soldier over suspected Russian spying as US indicts Iranian cell for RAF Fairford plot

British counter-terrorism officers have arrested a 41-year-old senior United States Army soldier in Gloucestershire on suspicion of spying for Russia, following a joint operation with MI5, UK Defence Counter Intelligence, US Army Counterintelligence Command and the FBI. Stationed at Imjin Barracks in Innsworth—headquarters of Nato’s Allied Rapid Reaction Corps—the serviceman was detained near Gloucester on Tuesday and taken to a London police station under sections one and three of the National Security Act 2023, which cover disclosing protected information and assisting a foreign intelligence service and allow detention for up to 14 days without charge. Officers searched two Gloucestershire properties as FBI director Kash Patel noted the bureau has made 167 espionage arrests over the past 21 months, up 53%. (Guardian, BBC)

Hours later in New York, federal prosecutors unsealed an eight-count indictment charging three operatives linked to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps and Iraqi militia Kata’ib Hezbollah with orchestrating September’s foiled bomb plot at RAF Fairford in Gloucestershire, the European base for American B-1 bombers during the war in Iran. Prosecutors allege that dual Iranian-Iraqi national Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, already held in a New York jail awaiting trial over 18 European attacks under the front group Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya—including seven in the UK and April’s stabbing of two Jewish men in Golders Green—used coded family phone calls to direct IRGC operative Mohsen Mohajeri and Iraqi citizen Mohammad Ali al-Hassani. The cell allegedly surveilled Fairford and sought vans, fuel barrels, chemical accelerants and shrapnel before a farmer spotted three suspicious vans near Whelford on 27 September, prompting UK arrests and the withdrawal of US bombers last month. (Guardian, BBC)

Two further security and military cases surfaced in London on Wednesday. Former parliamentary researcher Chris Cash, acquitted in the Westminster China spy case after the prosecution collapsed, shared more than 6,000 messages showing how his friend in China, Chris Berry, relayed inquiries from a senior Chinese official during the 2022 Tory leadership race about whether a sanctioned MP might enter the cabinet; Cash admitted his Westminster gossip was naive, yet insisted he received no Chinese money and was made a fall guy. Meanwhile, the inquiry into UK special forces in Afghanistan released photographs from two 2011 SAS night raids in Helmand that killed 17 people, including boys aged 14 and 15. Lead counsel Oliver Glasgow KC said the images—showing unarmed people lying on pillows and under blankets with head wounds and low wall blood spatter—contradicted SAS accounts and pointed to possible executions while asleep, a view backed by military police investigator Lt Col John Harvey. (BBC, BBC)

David Walliams accused of preying on young women and teenagers after High Court rejects anonymity bid

Comedian, children’s author and former Britain’s Got Talent judge David Walliams has been accused by multiple women of exploiting his celebrity status and workplace authority to groom teenage fans and pursue young women for sex. Accounts gathered from more than 30 first-hand sources in an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News include two women, now in their 30s, who met the 55-year-old star when they were 15 and allege he groomed them in ways that affected them for nearly two decades. Other women allege inappropriate conduct connected to Britain’s Got Talent and a sexual relationship with a junior employee at his former publisher, HarperCollins. Walliams denies all wrongdoing, saying he has never broken the law or acted as a sexual predator. (Guardian, BBC)

The findings were published after Mr Justice Nicklin dismissed an unprecedented High Court bid by Walliams—anonymised in court as PPT—for a lifelong injunction blocking publication. Rather than claiming breach of privacy, his barrister, Sara Mansoori KC, argued under Articles 2 and 3 of the European Convention on Human Rights that publication threatened his life after he made suicide attempts in May and July and was sectioned in a psychiatric hospital the week before the hearing. Nicklin ruled that hospital clinicians, rather than a civil court weighing press freedom under Article 10, bore the state’s duty to protect him, and Walliams confirmed on Monday he would not appeal. On Wednesday, presenter Jonathan Ross said he was horrified by both the Walliams allegations and the ten-and-a-half-year rape sentence handed to Russell Brand on Monday, while Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy condemned industry power imbalances, the Metropolitan Police confirmed several more people had come forward with potential criminal complaints against Brand, and Education Secretary Lucy Powell criticised the cross-examination of Brand’s victims. (Guardian, BBC, Guardian)

US judge allows Trump’s $10bn BBC defamation suit to proceed as House Republicans block Hegseth impeachment

A federal judge in Florida has ruled that Donald Trump’s $10bn (£7.5bn) defamation lawsuit against the BBC can go ahead, partially denying the broadcaster’s motion to dismiss over its Panorama documentary Trump: A Second Chance. The programme spliced together two remarks from Trump’s 6 January 2021 speech in Washington delivered nearly 55 minutes apart into a 12-second clip—an edit for which the BBC apologised after acknowledging it gave the mistaken impression of a direct call for violence. While US District Judge Jeffrey T Kuntz, a Trump appointee, dismissed a parallel claim under Florida’s unfair trade practices law because the broadcast was not commercial speech, he ruled that bridging a 55-minute gap went beyond routine condensation and sufficed at the pleading stage to allege actual malice. The BBC vowed to contest the case, which requires Trump to prove damages from a programme not aired in Florida and sit for a sworn deposition by 11 December. (Guardian, BBC)

In Washington, House Republicans closed ranks a week after losing both chambers in the midterms to table outgoing Kentucky Republican Thomas Massie’s resolution to impeach Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth over civilian deaths in Iran, unauthorised operations in Venezuela and Yemen, and retaliation against a Democratic senator. Republicans voted 211–204, with Massie the sole GOP dissenter, to refer the articles to the judiciary committee, though incoming Democratic Speaker Hakeem Jeffries called Hegseth the architect of a reckless war of choice and signalled Democrats will revisit his removal in January. Across the Potomac, nine Kennedy family members—excluding Health Secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr—joined lawsuits by Virginia and Washington DC to halt Trump’s planned 250ft triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery, arguing it would cast a shadow over John F Kennedy’s grave. (Guardian, BBC)

Labour MPs challenge Burnham’s 10-year industrial plan as Louise Casey warns England’s social care has no one in charge

Labour MPs from industrial and former red wall seats are meeting Cabinet Office minister Sally Jameson on Wednesday to warn that Prime Minister Andy Burnham’s 10-year plan for government lacks the teeth needed to halt deindustrialisation. Led by Andy MacNae and Jonathan Hinder, the Reindustrialisation Research Group argues that heavy industry is being crushed by high energy prices and that early briefings on the blueprint—which covers public ownership of utilities, lower household bills and a national care service, but has been delayed until January—fall short of Chancellor John Healey’s promise of a new industrial age. Their warning follows a London School of Economics lecture on Tuesday by Cabinet Secretary Antonia Romeo, attended by Burnham and Deputy Prime Minister Louise Haigh, in which Whitehall’s top official called the civil service too tame, reactive and risk-averse and pledged performance bonuses, tougher management of poor delivery and less sideways job-hopping ahead of a spring review. (Guardian, Guardian)

Public services and rural estates face sharp warnings elsewhere on Wednesday. Addressing the annual children and adult services conference, Baroness Louise Casey, chair of the adult social care commission, warns that successive governments have been asleep at the wheel, leaving millions reliant on an under-regulated postcode lottery dominated by private providers where nobody is in charge. Burnham has accelerated Casey’s review to 2027 and plans to fund a Scottish-style National Care Service by scrapping the state pension triple lock in the next parliament. Meanwhile, the Tenant Farmers Association warned that up to 40 holdings across Devon, Cornwall, Herefordshire and the Midlands face sell-offs as Prince William’s Duchy of Cornwall disposes of up to 20% of its 51,800-hectare estate over ten years to raise £500m for community and environmental projects, leaving Bradninch and Duloe tenants fearing they must buy their farms or leave; and the Office for Students warned that unsupervised assessments at 93 UK universities let students pass coursework in minutes using undetectable artificial intelligence. (Guardian, BBC, BBC)

Israeli opposition moves to seize Knesset agenda as UN chief presses Cop31 hosts on fossil fuel phase-out

Israel’s six opposition parties moved immediately after Tuesday’s swearing-in of the new Knesset to wrest control of the parliamentary agenda from caretaker prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu, while former military chief Gadi Eisenkot begins a six-week mandate to form a coalition. Opposition lawmakers tabled bills to establish a state inquiry into the 7 October 2023 attacks, repeal Netanyahu’s judicial overhaul and impose prime ministerial term limits that would bar Netanyahu—who has ruled for 19 of the past 30 years—from returning to office, while scheduling a vote next Tuesday to replace speaker Amir Ohana. Netanyahu used the ceremony to label lawmakers from two Palestinian-led opposition parties terror supporters and repeat baseless claims of ballot fraud in Arab communities, prompting walkouts by Democrats leader Yair Golan and former police chief Yoav Segalovich. (Guardian)

At the Cop31 summit in Antalya, outgoing UN Secretary-General António Guterres joined former US climate envoy John Kerry and Brazilian negotiators on Tuesday to urge co-hosts Turkey and Australia to turn Brazil’s post-Cop30 fossil fuel transition roadmap into concrete financing before 90 world leaders, including Burnham, Anthony Albanese and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, speak on Wednesday and Thursday, as World Meteorological Organization data confirmed 2026 will cap the four hottest years on record at 1.47C above pre-industrial levels. Elsewhere, Ukraine’s I Want to Live project announced the capture in Zaporizhzhia of its first Indonesian prisoner of war—a 49-year-old from Java—after Russian recruiters lured 283 Indonesians in 2026 via fake job ads; and in Hamburg, Attorney General Ellie Reeves told the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea that Argentina’s bid to halt March 2027 drilling at the Sea Lion oilfield was a disguised sovereignty claim that would cost Falkland Islanders billions of pounds. (Guardian, Meio, Guardian, Guardian)

Brazil’s Federal Police rift deepens over Banco Master removals as electoral court fines Meta R$7.5m

The removal of two senior Federal Police commissioners who investigated ties between Banco Master controller Daniel Vorcaro and three Supreme Court justices has triggered an institutional rupture inside Brazil’s federal police. Director-general Andrei Rodrigues resigned from the National Association of Federal Police Commissioners (ADPF) on Tuesday after the body condemned Monday’s dismissal of anti-corruption and Supreme Court inquiries chiefs Daniel Mostardeiro Cola and Wedson Cajé Lopes as retaliation, while Transparency International Brazil warned the removals carried extreme gravity. Meanwhile, a confidential spin-off from the Supreme Court’s newly archived seven-year fake news inquiry—examining leaked Federal Revenue tax records of justices and their relatives—was reassigned to Justice André Mendonça, Senate President Davi Alcolumbre praised Chief Justice Edson Fachin’s closure of the main probe as he seeks re-election, and Justice Luiz Fux suspended lower-court lawsuits nationwide challenging the provisional measure banning online sports betting and virtual casinos. (Folha, Folha, Folha, Meio)

In electoral law, the Superior Electoral Court (TSE) voted unanimously on Tuesday night to fine Meta R$7.5m (£1m) for failing to ensure equal treatment between President Lula and Senator Flávio Bolsonaro on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp during the presidential campaign. In the Chamber of Deputies, Centrão party leaders told Speaker Hugo Motta that their caucuses had rebelled against a deal to introduce mixed-district voting from 2034—originally intended to curb Liberal Party vote-pullers such as Nikolas Ferreira and Lucas Pavanato, who each won over three million votes this year—forcing negotiators to consider higher electoral thresholds instead. Separately, a Brasília federal court ordered the Caixa Econômica Federal to release R$2.42m from the 2018 auction of the Guarujá triplex to the former OAS group, now Grupo Metha, ruling that no criminal claim remained over the flat once attributed to Lula under Operation Car Wash. (Folha, Folha, Folha)

Economy

Anthropic trims Wall Street IPO target to $1.4tn as Niesr warns Bank of England rate caution risks sticky inflation

Artificial intelligence developer Anthropic is seeking a valuation of up to $1.4tn (£1.1tn) in next week’s Wall Street flotation, scaling back earlier expectations of a $2tn debut after US midterm victories for anti-datacentre candidates sharpened investor doubts over returns on AI infrastructure. According to a Tuesday filing, the San Francisco creator of Claude aims to raise up to $64.4bn by selling 825 million shares at $70 to $78, alongside a $26bn private placement with Alphabet and Nvidia and a $9.7bn greenshoe option that could lift total proceeds to $100bn—surpassing the $75bn raised when Elon Musk’s SpaceX listed at $1.78tn. Chief executive Dario Amodei and six co-founders are each selling $260m in stock while keeping stakes above $18bn. Meanwhile, Nvidia—down $500bn in value since Friday—hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, led by partner Joon Kim, to investigate chief executive Jensen Huang’s affair with Megaspeed executive and suspected Chinese operative Alice Huang. (Guardian, BBC)

In Britain, the National Institute of Economic and Social Research (Niesr) warned on Wednesday that the Bank of England’s quarter-point rate rise from 3.75% to 4% last week risks leaving inflation above its 2% target until at least 2030. With inflation at 3.5% and forecast by Niesr director David Aikman to top 4% in early 2027 as pay deals are set, the thinktank argued further hikes are needed even after Brent crude dipped below $90 a barrel on Tuesday. Higher borrowing costs, stamp duty of up to 19% for overseas buyers and the end of non-dom status are also squeezing London’s luxury property sector: researcher Molior counted 1,400 unsold new flats in Zone 1 at the end of September, triple the 2016 total, while housing starts fell 75% to 1,600 and developers London Richmond and Ardmore Construction entered administration. Elsewhere, Aldi is cutting up to 150 UK tech roles after 103 finance redundancies and outsourcing work to India via Genpact as UK sales growth slowed to 0.4%, while the Access to Medicine Foundation warned that pharma firms’ focus on GLP-1 weight-loss drugs—which just received US FDA warnings over sudden vision loss—risks starving poorer nations of insulin. (Guardian, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

Technology

Apple probes fatal gas leak at Indian iPhone plant, closes 28-year support forums and reveals PROLED MacBook Pro internals

Apple has sent investigators to a Tata Electronics component plant in Hosur, Tamil Nadu, after three contract workers died from inhaling gas while inspecting an external nano-filtration tank at an effluent treatment facility operated by Nalco Water. While production at the site—part of an Indian supply chain assembling roughly a quarter of global iPhones—was paused for Deepavali, the fatal accident hit the same complex where pollution regulators and health officials investigated farmland water contamination complaints earlier this year. Separately on Tuesday night, Apple placed its Apple Support Community forums into read-only mode ahead of their permanent closure on 20 November, retiring a user troubleshooting platform launched as Apple Tech Exchange in 1998. (9to5Mac, MacMagazine, 9to5Mac)

Across the ecosystem, an iFixit teardown of the touchscreen MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display showed how Apple cut the 14-inch laptop’s weight from 1.55kg to 1.38kg, used larger blue subpixels in its dual-layer tandem OLED panel to extend display life, and revived the glowing lid logo with four LEDs, a diffuser and a two-way mirror coating—while letting swapped logic boards pass Touch ID calibration. Leaks also revealed a Claris-branded Mac app called Harbor that pools unified memory across multiple Macs over Thunderbolt 5 to run local open-weight AI models, while Apple TV adds toggleable American and British Sign Language overlays on Friday starting with Being Heumann and F1: The Movie, and Edovia’s Screens 5.10 brought macOS High Performance screen sharing and audio streaming to iPhone and iPad. Beyond Apple, smart-ring maker Oura agreed to buy medical AI startup Counsel Health for $625m, Adobe unveiled Firefly timeline video generation and Topaz upscaling at Adobe MAX, and Google DeepMind used agentic AI to formally verify the cryptographic security of the Signal protocol used by Signal, WhatsApp and Google Messages. (9to5Mac, 9to5Mac, MacStories, MacStories, The Verge, 9to5Mac)

GTA 6 breaks PlayStation and Xbox pre-order records as 30fps cap divides players and Sony cancels Fairgames

Sony and Microsoft confirmed on Tuesday that Grand Theft Auto VI is the most pre-ordered game in the history of both the PlayStation Store and Microsoft Store, with Sensor Tower estimating advance sales at 9.69 million units—beating Cyberpunk 2077—as console pre-loading opened ahead of the 19 November launch. Both companies urged players to pre-load early to avoid server bottlenecks, while Logitech introduced a Logi Game Day holiday letting staff take launch day off. Alongside a trailer showing SWAT raids and Vice City clubs, Rockstar confirmed GTA 6 will target 30 frames per second across all consoles, including PS5 Pro—which gets ray-traced shadows and PSSR upscaling rather than 60fps—and stream to Xbox One via Xbox Cloud Gaming. Meanwhile, Sony cancelled Haven Studios’ live-service heist shooter Fairgames after weak playtests, reassigning the Montreal team without layoffs and announcing the PlayStation Plus PC app will close on 10 December because under 0.4% of Premium members use it. (IGN, IGN, IGN, The Verge, The Verge)

Culture

Booker winner M John Harrison warns of societal confusion as Old Vic unveils 2027 season and Stacy Keach dies at 85

Speaking the morning after becoming the Booker Prize’s oldest laureate at 81—and its first science-fiction winner—for his 13th novel The End of Everything, M John Harrison warned that societies are dream-walking into a desperate situation marked by epistemological collapse. Begun after the 2008 crash and expanded after Harrison survived a heart attack at a 2015 east London reading, the Kent-set novel follows characters navigating a fracturing Britain alongside luminous beings called the iGhettis—a pun blending capitalism, Getty wealth, Apple tech and ego—while withholding neat explanations. Across the Thames at the Old Vic, incoming artistic director Rupert Goold unveiled his inaugural 2027 season, opening on 26 January with Damian Lewis as Henry V in his first major stage role in nearly a decade, followed by Supergirl star Milly Alcock in Rebecca Frecknall’s adaptation of Miss Julie, Stephen Sondheim’s Assassins, and Arinzé Kene in Kohlhaas, backed by £20 front-row preview tickets. (Guardian, Guardian)

The acting world also mourned American star Stacy Keach, who died at home in Magdalenka, Poland, on Tuesday aged 85 after heart failure. Trained at Berkeley, Yale and Lamda as a Fulbright scholar, Keach played Hamlet, Richard III and King Lear onstage, won a Golden Globe as Ernest Hemingway, worked twice with John Huston in Fat City and The Life and Times of Judge Roy Bean, and appeared in The Ninth Configuration, American History X, Nebraska and Jay Kelly, while finding television fame as Mickey Spillane’s detective Mike Hammer—a run interrupted in 1984 when he served six months in Reading prison after being arrested at Heathrow with cocaine in a shaving cream can. (Guardian)

Manchester United chiefs convene in Monaco over Carrick as Pochettino eyes return and Kane nears England cap record

Manchester United chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox fly to Monaco on Wednesday for a summit with minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe expected to seal the sacking of head coach Michael Carrick, with United 18th in the Premier League after one win in ten games. US men’s national team coach Mauricio Pochettino is keen on moving to Old Trafford—an interest described as mutual—though prising the Argentine from his contract through 2030 ahead of Concacaf Nations League games against Haiti would cost US Soccer’s $10m (£7.5m) release clause plus compensation for staff led by Jesús Pérez. Meanwhile, bottom club Crystal Palace could avoid a hefty payout to departing manager Pierre Sage—whom they decided to sack after Sunday’s 3-1 loss to Liverpool, with Thomas Frank favourite to replace him—after Lens sacked Yannick Cahuzac on Tuesday following a 9-1 Champions League defeat by Como and moved to rehire Sage; and Football Leaks founder Rui Pinto has opened talks via lawyer William Bourdon with the Serious Fraud Office over a cooperation deal following Manchester City’s financial charges ruling, as he fights the removal of his Portuguese witness protection. (BBC, Guardian, Guardian, Guardian)

In international football, England captain Harry Kane prepares to win his 126th cap against Croatia at Wembley on Thursday—passing Peter Shilton as England’s most-capped men’s player two weeks after winning the Ballon d’Or—crediting his improved sprint metrics at 33 to giving up post-match Haribo sweets, drinking bone broth and having monthly electrical acupuncture with specialist Alejandro Elorriaga Claraco. In Glasgow, Scotland midfielder Scott McTominay revealed ahead of Friday’s match against North Macedonia that his absence before June’s World Cup opener against Haiti in Boston was caused by an irregular heartbeat: the 29-year-old Napoli player was sedated in hospital 48 hours before kick-off to have his heart electrically shocked back into rhythm before surgery in September. (Guardian, Guardian)
